title: Type Constraints
concept: Type constraints (T: Interface) restrict type parameters to types that implement specific interfaces — ensuring generic code can use needed operations.
why: Without constraints, you can't call methods or use operators on generic types. Constraints tell the compiler what operations are available.
theory:
## Bounding Type Parameters

### Why Constraints?
```xiom
fn print[T](value: T) {
  io.println(value.to_str());  // ERROR: T might not have to_str()
}
```

### With Constraints
```xiom
fn print[T: Display](value: T) {
  io.println(value.to_str());  // OK: T: Display guarantees to_str()
}
```

### Common Constraints
| Constraint | Enables |
|-----------|---------|
| T: Eq | ==, != |
| T: Ord | <, >, <=, >= |
| T: Display | .to_str() |
| T: Clone | .clone() |
| T: Hash | .hash() |
| T: Default | Default::default() |
| T: Copy | Bitwise copy |

### Multiple Constraints on One Param
```xiom
fn sort_and_format[T: Ord + Display](items: &Vec[T]) -> Str {
  var sorted = items.clone();
  sorted.sort();  // T: Ord
  return sorted[0].to_str();  // T: Display
}
```

### Different Constraints per Param
```xiom
fn print_map[K: Display, V: Display](map: &Map[K, V]) {
  for (k, v) in map {
    io.println(k.to_str() + " -> " + v.to_str());  // Both K and V need Display
  }
}
```
syntax_ref:
fn name[T: Interface](param: T) { /* can use Interface methods on T */ }
fn name[T: Interface1 + Interface2](param: T) { /* T must satisfy both */ }
tips: Start with minimal constraints — only add what your function actually needs
Remember: T: Ord implies T: Eq (ordering requires equality)
The compiler tells you EXACTLY which constraint you're missing — read the error message
Prefer interface constraints over concrete types — T: Display, not T: Str
common_mistakes: Forgetting to add constraints — the compiler will help you, but it's good to think ahead
Adding unnecessary constraints — T: Ord when you only use == (use T: Eq instead)
Using concrete types as constraints — that defeats the purpose of generics
